title: goworker
description: Client sync, inbound /send, federation reads, the outbound federation sender and event creation, in one process. Every panel of the dashboards it replaces is here (goevent-creator's shadow panels excepted: there is no shadow mode): a part nginx or homeserver.yaml gives no work shows empty panels.

list.name: Worker restarts
list.expr: changes(process_start_time_seconds{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[2m]) > 0 and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}

list.name: synapse_server
list.label: Synapse server_name
list.description: Synapse's own metrics, for the comparison panels.

list.name: synapse_inbound_job
list.label: Synapse inbound worker job
list.description: The Python inbound federation worker, for the comparison panels.

panels.title: Sending federation
panels.description: 1 while homeserver.yaml names this instance in federation_sender_instances. 0 is normal for a worker that is not the sender.

panels.title: Senders named
panels.description: How many federation_sender_instances homeserver.yaml lists: the number of shards destinations are split into.

panels.title: /send answered here
panels.description: Share of /send transactions answered here rather than by main.

panels.title: Reads answered here
panels.description: Share of federation reads answered natively. The rest fell back to main.

panels.title: Sync 5xx
panels.description: Share of client sync requests answered 5xx (499, the client hanging up, excluded).

panels.title: Replication connected
panels.description: The one subscription to Synapse's replication stream that every part reads.

panels.title: Limits refusing (window)
panels.description: Requests refused because a limit was full. See Memory & limits.

panels.title: Degraded
panels.description: Parts that could not start and whose requests go to main (goworker_degraded). Each one is logged at start.

panels.title: homeserver.yaml reloads (window)
panels.description: Changes to homeserver.yaml picked up at runtime. An error keeps the last good copy.

panels.title: Heap against the memory limit
panels.description: Heap in use and RSS against memory.limit_mb. The collector works harder as the heap nears the limit; RSS lags the heap after a drop.

targets.expr: go_memstats_heap_inuse_bytes and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}
process_resident_memory_bytes and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}

panels.title: Cache bytes
panels.description: The byte-bounded caches. state_groups is the one state cache, shared by the federation reads and inbound write mode (memory.state_cache_mb).

panels.title: Goroutines and GC
panels.description: Goroutines are cheap and spawned freely; a steady climb is a leak, not load.

targets.expr: go_goroutines and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}
rate(go_gc_duration_seconds_count{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket]) and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}

panels.title: Slots in use by limit
panels.description: Work holding a slot, by limit; a line at its capacity is a limit binding.

panels.title: Wait for a slot (p99)
panels.description: Zero waits are observed too, so this is meaningful at low traffic.

panels.title: Lines read and reconnects
panels.description: One subscription for the whole process. Each reconnect empties and re-arms every cache that depends on the stream.

panels.title: Lines waiting per consumer
panels.description: Each part reads through its own queue. A queue that climbs is a part falling behind; at its bound it is resynced.

panels.title: Consumer resyncs
panels.description: A part fell a whole queue behind and started over, as if its connection had dropped.

targets.expr: rate(process_cpu_seconds_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket]) and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}

panels.title: Open file descriptors
panels.description: Thousands is normal: one connection per remote server being sent to.

targets.expr: process_open_fds and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}
changes(process_start_time_seconds{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket]) and on (job, instance) goworker_build_info{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}

panels.title: Resident memory
panels.description: Watch the trend across days, not the value. The state caches fill as rooms are touched and then plateau; a line that never flattens is the thing to report.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: Roughly two per parked long poll plus the replication subscriber. Should fall back when clients disconnect -- if it does not, that is a leak.

targets.expr: sum(go_goroutines{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"} and on(instance, job) gosync_build_info)

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Days, not minutes: this is the panel a soak is for.

panels.title: CPU
panels.description: Fraction of one core. A parked long poll costs nothing, so this should sit near zero between wakeups and rise while a sync is built. Sustained load with no traffic means work is happening off the request path -- the typing hot loop looked exactly like that, at 15%. GC is drawn alongside so a rise can be attributed: the Go client does not export a user/system split on Linux, so that is not available here.

panels.title: Goroutines and waiters
panels.description: These two should move together. Goroutines climbing while waiters do not is a leak in something other than the long poll.

targets.expr: sum(go_goroutines{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"} and on(instance, job) gosync_build_info)

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Resident memory. The point of consolidating workers is a lower total than the Python fleet it replaces.

panels.title: GC pause
panels.description: Stop-the-world pause time. A large shared state cache shows up here first.

panels.title: Goroutines
panels.description: One goroutine per destination with work is the bet this worker is built on, so this is that bet in numbers. Read it against 'destinations with queued work': goroutines should track it, plus a small constant. Wake spawns before taking a concurrency slot, so this can legitimately exceed queue.max_concurrent_destinations -- the excess is goroutines parked waiting for a slot, not sends in flight. A count that climbs while queued work does not is a leak.

panels.title: Memory
panels.description: Resident is what the host sees; heap in-use is what Go is holding. The gap between heap in-use and heap allocated is memory Go has freed but not returned to the OS, so resident lags a drop in real usage by minutes -- expect it after a large queue is dropped rather than reading it as a leak. Stack in-use is roughly the goroutine count times 8-16KB, and is the direct cost of the concurrency model.

panels.title: Open file descriptors
panels.description: One per open connection, so this tracks how many remote servers are being talked to at once. Plotted against the process limit because exhausting it does not look like a resource problem from the outside -- it looks like every destination failing at once, which reads as a network outage.

panels.title: Requests
panels.description: Requests served per second, all four endpoints.

panels.title: 5xx ratio
panels.description: Share of requests that failed on our side. Anything sustained above zero is a bug, not load. Reads 0 rather than "No data" when it has never happened: for a panel whose healthy value is zero, those two must not look the same.

targets.expr: (sum(rate(gosync_requests_total{endpoint=~"$sync_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", status=~"5.."}[$bucket])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min(sum(rate(gosync_requests_total{endpoint=~"$sync_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])) or vector(0), 0.0001)

panels.title: Long polls parked
panels.description: Clients currently waiting for something to happen. On a worker serving real clients this is the steady state: idle syncs, not idle CPU. Zero with clients connected means they are not reaching us.

panels.title: Replication
panels.description: The gauge that matters. While this is 0 the worker cannot report typing at all and its stream positions are only as fresh as the last database seed -- and /health will still say ok, because it does not check this.

panels.title: Database role
panels.description: 1 when the main pool's role cannot write. To-device deletion uses a separate role and a separate pool, so this staying at 1 is expected even with to_device enabled.

panels.title: Version
panels.description: Tag the running image was built from.

panels.title: Requests by endpoint
panels.description: Element Web drives /sync almost exclusively; the three legacy endpoints should be flat at zero unless something is deliberately calling them.

panels.title: Duration percentiles
panels.description: READ THIS CAREFULLY: a /sync that waits the client's full timeout and returns nothing is a SUCCESS, and it lands at 30s. High percentiles here are the normal shape of a healthy long-polling endpoint. What matters is the LOW end -- an initial sync or a sync with news should be well under a second.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gosync_request_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$sync_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gosync_request_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$sync_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gosync_request_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$sync_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))

panels.title: Outcomes
panels.description: served / refused / client_gone. A client hanging up mid-long-poll is ORDINARY for /sync -- Element does it on every navigation -- and is deliberately not counted as an error.

panels.title: Status codes
panels.description: 401 and 403 are the client's problem; 5xx is ours. A burst of 502 means whoami could not reach Synapse -- the worker refuses to guess rather than logging clients out.

panels.title: Long polls parked
panels.description: Should track the number of connected clients, and should return to that level after every wakeup. A sawtooth that never comes back down is a leak.

panels.title: Duration distribution
panels.description: Expect two clusters on a live worker: fast responses at the bottom, and a band at the client's timeout where idle long polls expire. A spreading middle is where trouble shows.

panels.title: Requests by status and endpoint
panels.description: The same counter split both ways, for when one endpoint misbehaves and the others do not.

panels.title: Token cache
panels.description: Cached token verdicts. Bounded by auth.max_entries.

panels.title: Rejections
panels.description: Tokens Synapse said no to. Reads 0 rather than "No data" when it has never happened: for a panel whose healthy value is zero, those two must not look the same.

panels.title: Whoami unavailable
panels.description: The one to watch: Synapse could not be asked. The worker answers 502 and NEVER 401, because refusing a valid token would log real clients out. Sustained non-zero means the whoami socket is wrong or the client-API worker is down. Reads 0 rather than "No data" when it has never happened: for a panel whose healthy value is zero, those two must not look the same.

panels.title: Verdicts
panels.description: accepted / rejected / missing / unavailable.

panels.title: Checked natively
panels.description: 1: access tokens are checked here, as Synapse's InternalAuth does. 0: every token goes to main's /whoami -- the log line "client auth: every token goes to /whoami" says why (MAS, account_validity, modules, an unreadable registration, no database).

panels.title: Answered by /whoami
panels.description: The share of authenticated requests main answered: guests' macaroons, wrong tokens, an appservice whose regex RE2 cannot compile. Native, this should be near 0.

targets.expr: sum(rate(goworker_client_auth_verdicts_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", source="whoami"}[$bucket])) / sum(rate(goworker_client_auth_verdicts_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", source!=""}[$bucket])) or vector(0)

panels.title: USER_IP not sent
panels.description: USER_IP commands failed or dropped: main then has no record of those clients' last-seen address and user agent. Reads 0 rather than "No data" when it has never happened.

panels.title: Client auth verdicts by source
panels.description: Every client-API part's authentication (platform/clientauth): accepted, rejected, or unknown (database or main unreachable, answered 502), by where the answer came from.

panels.title: Client auth queries (p99)
panels.description: Round trips to authenticate a request whose lookups were not cached: token (_query_for_auth), user (locked, exists), device (an appservice's ?device_id=), mark_used (a token's first use).

panels.title: Client auth invalidations and USER_IP
panels.description: Cached lookups dropped because Synapse invalidated them on the caches stream (a logout, a lock), or all at once on a reconnect (purge); and USER_IP commands by outcome.

panels.title: Deleted in range
panels.description: Messages this worker has deleted from device_inbox over the dashboard's time range. This is the only write it makes. Zero with an encrypted client connected means to_device is disabled -- and that client will never receive room keys.

panels.title: Deletion rate
panels.description: Deletion is bounded by each client's own `since`, so this should track how fast messages arrive for the devices syncing here. A rate far above that means something is acknowledging on a client's behalf.

panels.title: Queries per request
panels.description: Database round trips per client request. THE number this worker is optimised for: its cost is round trips, not database seconds. A quiet incremental sync should sit near 18; it was 688 before the query work.

panels.title: Query rate
panels.description: Queries issued to Synapse's PostgreSQL, per second.

panels.title: Cache hit rate
panels.description: MISLEADING ON ITS OWN. A disarmed cache reports neither hits nor misses, so 'no data' here means the caches are switched off or replication is down -- not that they are useless. Read Caches armed beside it.

panels.title: Caches armed
panels.description: How many derived caches are serving. Anything below 7 means replication is down and the caches are refusing to answer rather than guessing. Alert on this, not on the hit rate.

panels.title: Cache purges
panels.description: Rows on Synapse's caches stream treated as destructive. Should be at or near ZERO. That stream carries a row every couple of seconds, almost all of it about caches this worker does not hold; an earlier build treated every row as destructive and emptied the state caches continuously, costing 4,910 extra queries on one initial sync. Reads 0 rather than 'No data' when there have been none, so a blank panel means the metric is missing, not that the count is zero.

panels.title: State cache entries
panels.description: Immutable state-group caches. These hold state groups, which never change, so they are always on -- unlike the derived caches.

panels.title: Queries by store method
panels.description: Which store method is talking to the database. The top entry is the next thing worth removing; a single method dominating usually means it is being asked once per room.

panels.title: Cache hits and misses
panels.description: Per cache. A cache with misses and no hits is either newly armed (a guarded cache does not answer until replication has caught up to the token) or genuinely useless -- check its entry count before concluding.

panels.title: Cache entries
panels.description: Entries held per derived cache. A cache pinned flat at its configured bound is evicting; raise it or accept the misses.

panels.title: Cache evictions
panels.description: Evictions per cache. Sustained eviction on room_summary means the account has more rooms than the cache is sized for.

panels.title: Caches stream, by action
panels.description: What we did with each row on Synapse's caches replication stream. 'ignored' should dominate: those rows concern caches this worker does not hold. 'purge' should be flat at zero.

panels.title: Row rate
panels.description: Replication rows received per second, every stream. This worker follows the whole channel, so this is the homeserver's activity, not ours.

panels.title: Global rows
panels.description: Share of rows that name neither a room nor a user, and therefore wake EVERY parked client. This is the panel that found the caches stream doing it about once a second: 94 of 95 global rows were that one stream, waking every client to recompute a sync that was always empty. Streams that wake nobody by design are counted scope="silent" and are not in this number.

targets.expr: (sum(rate(gosync_replication_rows_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance", scope="global"}[$bucket])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min(sum(rate(gosync_replication_rows_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])) or vector(0), 0.0001)

panels.title: Wakeups per row
panels.description: How many parked syncs the average replication row costs. Approaching the parked-client count means rows are waking everybody; near zero on an idle server is right.

targets.expr: (sum(rate(gosync_notifier_wakeups_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min(sum(rate(gosync_replication_rows_total{job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])) or vector(0), 0.0001)

panels.title: Wakeup rate
panels.description: Parked syncs woken per second. Each one recomputes a sync; most find nothing and park again.

panels.title: Writer restarts
panels.description: Replication positions that went BACKWARDS, in the dashboard range. A stream whose serial lives in a writer's memory -- typing is the only one served here -- restarts at zero when that worker does, and this is the only evidence it happened: rows keep arriving, wakeups keep firing, the connection stays healthy. Expect one per typing writer restart and none otherwise. Database-backed streams are not counted: a lower position from one of those is Synapse announcing max(writer position, persisted-up-to) and is ordinary traffic.

panels.title: Replication gaps
panels.description: POSITION commands claiming the stream had moved further than the rows we saw, in the dashboard range. Means rows were missed -- a disconnect, or a row that could not be parsed -- rather than merely being behind. Responses are read from the database so none of them is wrong because of this, but every stream-change cache below that position gives up its horizon, so a burst is followed by a burst of queries the gates would otherwise have skipped.

panels.title: Rows by stream
panels.description: Which streams carry the traffic. presence dominates on a federated server and is correctly targeted at one user per row.

panels.title: Wakeups by stream
panels.description: Which streams actually cost us work. A stream high here but low in Rows by stream is waking many clients per row -- that is the shape to investigate.

panels.title: Rows by scope
panels.description: Stacked. 'global' wakes every parked client and should be a thin band; 'silent' is a stream that wakes nobody by design -- the caches stream, which carries Synapse's own invalidations and appears in no stream token.

panels.title: Position discontinuities, by stream
panels.description: Where a restart or a gap actually landed. reset on `typing` is an EDU worker restart and is handled: the position is adopted and the typist map cleared; the other two resettable streams are a federation sender's business and this worker holds nothing from either. gap on any stream lines up with `gosync_replication_connected` dropping, or with an unparseable row -- if it does not, the row shapes in rowDetails have drifted from Synapse's.

panels.title: Client sync: Stream-change caches (the query gates)
Gate horizon lag
panels.description: gosync_stream_cache_earliest_position subtracted from the stream's current position: how far back each cache can answer. THIS IS THE PANEL THAT MATTERS. A cache too small for its stream has this shrink towards zero; every question then falls below the horizon, every gate answers 'changed', and the queries come back with no error and no wrong answer. A flat line at 0 for a stream means its cache is doing nothing. membership is measured against the events position because it has no stream of its own -- it is fed by m.room.member rows. It and account_data are armed empty and start at 0 lag by design; they fill from live traffic.

panels.title: Queries the gates skipped
panels.description: The payoff, read from the queries that did NOT run. PresenceSince is the expensive one: a correlated subquery over presence_stream and current_state_events, 25ms warm and 430ms cold, previously run once per sync whether or not any presence had moved. Compare against the sync rate: on a quiet server most syncs should run neither.

panels.title: Stream cache hits and misses
panels.description: A 'hit' is a question answered from memory, whether the answer was 'changed' or 'unchanged' -- so a high hit rate means the cache is working, not that queries were skipped. Use the skipped-queries panel for that. Misses are questions that fell below the horizon.

panels.title: Entities and positions held
panels.description: Positions is what the size bound limits, not entities: one stream position can name many rooms. Positions sitting exactly at the configured size means the cache is full and evicting.

panels.title: Evictions, and gates armed
panels.description: Evictions raise the horizon, which is how a too-small cache quietly stops working -- read this alongside the horizon-lag panel. Armed drops to 0 when replication is lost, at which point every gate answers 'changed' and the worker behaves exactly as it did before these caches existed. It also reads 0 for a cache configured to hold nothing, deliberately: that is indistinguishable from disarmed to every caller.

panels.title: Responses by outcome
panels.description: THE PANEL TO CHECK FIRST. `immediate` means there was news without waiting, `woken` means a parked poll was woken by it, `timed_out` means it waited to the deadline with nothing. A worker answering `immediate` on nearly every request has a broken emptiness rule, not a busy server -- on 2026-09-03 any present extension counted as news, so the long poll never waited and SchildiChat was answered about ten times a second per connection. Healthy shape: `woken` and `timed_out` carrying the traffic, `immediate` only as often as clients start new connections.

panels.title: Rooms per response
panels.description: After the first response for a connection, a quiet poll should describe ZERO rooms. A steady stream of full windows means every response re-sends everything, which is the difference between a sliding sync and a very expensive /sync.

panels.title: Connection-store writes
panels.description: This endpoint is the only one that writes. The write is proportional to the connection's ROOM COUNT rather than to what changed, because each new position copies the previous one's rows forward -- measured at ~725 stream rows plus ~248 room-config rows per position for a 654-room connection, times the three connections Element X holds per device. A quiet poll should write nothing: compare positions_minted against the response rate, and if they track each other the 'reuse the position when nothing changed' short-circuit has stopped working.

panels.title: Connection store size
panels.description: Small by design: reading a position deletes the other positions on its connection, and the reaper removes connections nobody uses. A row count that climbs steadily means one of those two has stopped -- `reaped` flat at zero for days is the reaper, and positions far above connections is the prune. Neither is visible any other way. `store_up` at 0 means the last scrape could not reach the database, so the other numbers here are stale.

panels.title: Response size
panels.description: A client controls its own window and required_state, so it controls this almost entirely. The expensive failure here is not a slow query but a client asking for a thousand rooms with ["*","*"].

panels.title: Unknown positions
panels.description: M_UNKNOWN_POS is a supported path, not an error: the client starts a fresh connection. A steady trickle is normal (9.3% of live requests already begin with no connection state). A SPIKE is not -- every connected client re-bootstrapping at once is what a schema change or a misconfigured reaper looks like.

panels.title: Relays vs suppressed
panels.description: The throttle at work. Suppressed should DWARF delivered -- clients sync in a loop and the writer's timers are far coarser, so one relay per device per 25s is enough. If the two lines converge, the throttle has stopped working and every sync is making an HTTP call to another worker on the request path.

panels.title: Relay failures by reason
panels.description: Each reason needs a different fix, which is why this is not one number. `refused` = the writer answered non-200, almost always a rotated worker_replication_secret. `unreachable` = nothing accepted the connection; the presence writer moved, or homeserver.yaml names a path this container cannot see. `timeout` = it accepted and did not answer, so it is overloaded rather than misconfigured. `client_gone` = the syncing client hung up, which is nobody's fault and is here so it cannot inflate the other three. Sustained non-zero on the first three means users this worker serves are drifting offline while their syncs look perfectly healthy.

panels.title: Relay latency
panels.description: This is the only synchronous outbound call on the sync path, so a slow presence writer makes THIS worker slow. It is a unix socket on the same host: p99 belongs in single-digit milliseconds. The 5s client timeout is the ceiling, and anything approaching it is already hurting the syncs that happen to land on a relay.

panels.title: Devices in the throttle
panels.description: One entry per (user, device) whose presence was relayed recently. It should track the number of distinct devices actually syncing and plateau. Growth without bound means entries are never dropped -- a leak in the map, not a busy server.

panels.title: Config re-reads after a failed presence relay
panels.description: homeserver.yaml re-read because a presence relay could not reach its writer, by outcome.

panels.title: Transactions/s
panels.description: Every /send this worker received, whatever it did with it.

panels.title: Answered natively
panels.description: Share of transactions answered here instead of by main. About 96% is the ceiling on this homeserver.

panels.title: Forward failures (window)
panels.description: EDUs that could not be handed to their stream writer. Each fails its transaction with a 500, and the sender retries.

panels.title: Upstream unreachable (window)
panels.description: Requests the Python inbound worker could not be reached for.

panels.title: Transactions by route and reason
panels.description: Where each transaction went (native, proxy, abandoned) and why. Proxy reasons: has_pdus (write mode unavailable), malformed, limits, auth_failed, origin_in_backoff, not_whitelisted, uncertain, db_error, too_large, not_send.

panels.title: Latency by route
panels.description: Time to answer, by route. Proxied latency is mostly the Python worker's.

panels.title: EDUs by type and action
panels.description: Every EDU decided: forwarded, dropped as untracked presence, or dropped by a room's server ACL. edu_type="other" is a type Synapse has no handler for; the log names the first of each.

panels.title: EDUs forwarded, by destination writer
panels.description: Forwards by stream writer. Set this beside the Synapse panel: the counts should match what the stream writers receive.

panels.title: Forward latency
panels.description: One EDU handed to its writer over replication, retries included.

panels.title: Forwards by outcome
panels.description: ok, error (a non-retryable answer) or timeout (gave up after retrying).

panels.title: Replication retries and ACL removals
panels.description: Retries of a forward (timeout or connection refused), and rooms removed from receipt EDUs by server ACL.

panels.title: Policy servers, and v2.1 set-order ties
panels.description: 'policy': what Synapse did with a room's policy server, against our verdict. 'policy_ask': our own request to the policy server, against Synapse's answer. Ties: v2.1 forwards reachability Synapse would compute differently in another process.

panels.title: Events handled by write mode
panels.description: Staged events by outcome: persisted, rejected and soft_failed (all three persisted); ignored, dropped and failed (persisted by nobody, as Synapse does; failed: auth raised, state groups stored); deferred and error (left staged for Synapse's worker).

panels.title: Write latency
panels.description: Deciding and persisting one event, and staging to unstaging (Synapse's pdu_process_time).

panels.title: Persister calls, device resyncs, pruning
panels.description: fed_send_events by persister and result (a conflict is a partial-state room un-partial-stated mid-way), its p99, device resyncs asked for, and events pruned from queues over 100.

panels.title: Origins in backoff marked as up
panels.description: write.mark_origins_up: an origin we had backed off sent us a transaction, so it was reset as Synapse's worker does (destinations, the caches stream row and its RDATA, REMOTE_SERVER_UP). db_error and publish_error send the next ones to Synapse for 5 minutes; 'proxied' is those, and every one while the setting is off.

panels.title: Inbound federation: Handing back to Synapse
Staging
panels.description: Events in federation_inbound_events_staging (ours and Synapse's) and the age of the oldest, at each minute's sweep; and the same for 'unattended' events, in rooms whose inbound lock no process holds. A busy room (Matrix HQ fetching missing prevs) can keep an event staged for many minutes while its holder works on it; an unattended one older than a minute or two means nobody will process it: with write.fallback: synapse, a Synapse process that is not sweeping (see the nudges).

panels.title: Events left or given up
panels.description: Staged events write mode deferred (left for Synapse) or, with write.fallback: none, gave up on and dropped after three attempts.

panels.title: Sweep nudges
panels.description: A copy of an answered transaction sent upstream on a deferral, so that Synapse starts its staged-events sweep. stored_answer is expected; other_answer means the upstream handled the copy instead of recognising it.

panels.title: Synapse: EDUs received over replication, by writer
panels.description: ReplicationFederationSendEduRestServlet on each Synapse instance: every EDU forwarded to it, from the Python worker or from us. Moving to native must not change this.

panels.title: Synapse: /send reaching the Python worker
panels.description: FederationSendServlet on the Python inbound worker. Falls by ~96% once EDU-only transactions are native.

panels.title: Synapse: inbound EDUs and PDUs at the Python worker
panels.description: What the Python worker still parses.

panels.title: Queries by name and result
panels.description: Every query is a primary-key lookup: txn_state once per native transaction, current_server_acl for typing and receipts (cached 5s per room), server_keys on a key-cache miss.

panels.title: ACL lookups by source
panels.description: cached, db, error, redacted (a redacted ACL sends the transaction to Synapse).

panels.title: State groups write mode needed
panels.description: From the one state cache shared with the federation reads: hit, rebuilt from a cached prev group (delta), or read whole (full).

panels.title: Expired origin keys
panels.description: Requests rejected because the origin's published key was past its valid_until_ts.

panels.title: Retry timings stored
panels.description: Destination retry timings written after our own outbound requests (store_retry_timings), by kind and outcome.

panels.title: Chain link batches per auth chain difference
panels.description: How many chain-link round trips one auth chain difference took (p50, p99).

panels.title: Request rate
panels.description: Federation requests served per second across all three endpoints.

panels.title: Failure ratio
panels.description: Share of requests returning 5xx. 502 means the upstream Synapse worker was unreachable, so a sustained non-zero value here is an availability problem, not a Matrix one.

panels.title: p99 upstream latency
panels.description: 99th percentile time waiting on Synapse. This is the baseline the native implementation has to beat.

panels.title: Upstream errors
panels.description: Rate of requests that could not reach any Synapse worker.

panels.title: Client disconnects
panels.description: Requests where the remote server hung up before we answered. Routine for slow /state calls; a spike suggests we became too slow for remote timeouts.

panels.title: Request rate by endpoint
panels.description: /state and /state_ids are the expensive ones; /event is usually the most frequent.

panels.title: Upstream latency percentiles
panels.description: Time spent waiting on the Synapse worker, by endpoint. NOTE: this covers every request, including cancelled ones. To compare against the native implementation use the 'Native vs Synapse latency' panel, which measures both over the same requests.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_upstream_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_upstream_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_upstream_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))

panels.title: Status codes
panels.description: 403 is normal federation traffic (server not in room, or barred by a server ACL). 404 on /event is normal too. Watch for 502 and 'none'.

panels.title: Requests by endpoint
panels.description: How each request was answered. During cutover this shows traffic shifting from proxy to native; a native fallback appears as proxy traffic on a native endpoint.

panels.title: Upstream latency distribution
panels.description: Full latency spread. Large rooms show up as a slow tail on /state.

panels.title: Response size percentiles
panels.description: /state on a large room returns megabytes of PDUs; this is what makes it costly.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_response_bytes_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_response_bytes_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))

panels.title: Upstream requests skipped
panels.description: Requests never forwarded because the client had already hung up -- work Synapse is spared, roughly 2.55s of its database time each on /state_ids. Deliberately separate from the cancelled-request count: a request cancelled after we forwarded is not work avoided.

panels.title: Clients that went away
panels.description: Remote servers hanging up. Routine for federation traffic and not a fault here -- Tuwunel-style servers hang up on /state_ids constantly -- but a sharp rise means something changed in how long we take to answer.

panels.title: Served natively
panels.description: Answers produced by us and sent to a remote server.

panels.title: Fell back to Synapse
panels.description: Requests we began but handed to main: auth_rejected (main answers the 401), timeout, error, client_gone.

panels.title: Fallback reasons
panels.description: Why a sampled request was not answered by us. client_gone means the remote server hung up before we could answer -- common here, since Tuwunel-style servers do it constantly, and not a defect. timeout means our own budget expired, which is worth investigating. auth_rejected means we could not verify the signature. error and panic point at our code.

panels.title: Native answer latency
panels.description: Time to produce an answer that was actually served, over the whole selected range rather than per bucket: at low volume a bucket with no observations yields NaN and draws as an empty panel.

panels.title: Fallback outcome at Synapse
panels.description: What happened at Synapse for requests we gave up on -- the question these metrics were added to answer. Without it a fallback was invisible past the moment it happened, because the upstream histogram covers every request and cannot isolate the abandoned one. upstream=canceled means the remote server had already gone, which on this deployment is the common case rather than the rare one.

targets.expr: sum by (endpoint, reason, upstream) (increase(gopro_native_fallback_upstream_total{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket]))

panels.title: What a fallback cost the client
panels.description: End-to-end time for a request that fell back: our attempt plus Synapse's, in series. This is why the serving budget (federation_reads.native_timeout_seconds) is short: the whole budget is spent before Synapse is even asked.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le, reason) (rate(gopro_native_fallback_total_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__range])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, reason) (rate(gopro_native_fallback_total_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__range])))

panels.title: Federation reads: Native performance (answers we served)
Native p50
panels.description: What a remote server waited for a median natively served request: verification plus the answer. Quantiles are taken over the whole selected range rather than per bucket: at this volume a bucket with no observations yields NaN and the panel draws empty. These series do not exist until the first answer is served natively, so this row is empty until nginx sends federation reads here, and after every restart until the first native answer.

panels.title: Native p90
panels.description: End-to-end, 90th percentile. Quantiles are taken over the whole selected range rather than per bucket: at this volume a bucket with no observations yields NaN and the panel draws empty.

panels.title: Native p99
panels.description: End-to-end, 99th percentile. This is the number to compare against Synapse's tail, which is where the advantage has always been -- not at p50.

panels.title: Answer p99
panels.description: The answer alone, excluding verification: state resolution, cache lookups and serialisation. This is the part we control and optimise. If it is flat while Native p99 rises, the cost is verification, not our code.

panels.title: Verification overhead
panels.description: Native p50 minus Answer p50, i.e. what X-Matrix verification costs a median request. Normally microseconds against a warm key cache; an origin whose keys must be fetched over the network costs a round trip, and against an unhealthy key server that has meant tens of seconds. Read it as an indication, not an exact figure: a difference of quantiles is not the quantile of differences.

targets.expr: (histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le) (rate(gopro_native_request_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__range])))) - (histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le) (rate(gopro_native_duration_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$__range]))))

panels.title: Served natively
panels.description: Answers produced by us and sent to a remote server.

panels.title: Native latency percentiles by endpoint
panels.description: End-to-end time for requests we served, per endpoint. Log scale, because p50 and p99 differ by orders of magnitude. Uses $bucket rather than the full range so change over time is visible; if it draws empty, widen $bucket. These series do not exist until the first native answer, so this is empty until nginx sends federation reads here.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_native_request_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.9, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_native_request_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_native_request_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))

panels.title: Where the time goes: verification vs answer
panels.description: The gap between the two pairs is X-Matrix verification. gopro_native_duration_seconds times only the answer, which is the part we optimise but not the part a remote server waits for -- verification sits in front of it and needs a network key fetch for any origin whose keys are not cached. The rate limiter is outside both: it is acquired before the attempt begins and is measured separately by gopro_rate_limit_queue_wait_seconds, so this gap is verification and nothing else.

panels.title: Native latency distribution
panels.description: Full spread of what remote servers waited for. A bimodal picture means cache hits and misses are resolving very differently -- expected on /state_ids, where a cold large room is orders of magnitude slower than a warm one.

panels.title: Native answers served
panels.description: Throughput of what we answered, by endpoint and status. 403 and 404 are ordinary federation outcomes here (a host not in the room, or an event we do not have), not errors. Falling back to Synapse is counted separately and does not appear as a status.

panels.title: Rejected (429)
panels.description: Requests refused outright. If this is non-zero while Synapse is not answering 429, our rc_federation is tighter than Synapse's and we are shedding load it would serve. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Delayed
panels.description: Requests deliberately slowed rather than refused. Throttling starts here, well before any rejection, so this is the earlier warning of the two. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Origins rejected
panels.description: Distinct servers rejected since startup. Answers whether throttling is one noisy server or many, which the counters alone cannot say. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Servers tracked
panels.description: Origin servers with live limiter state. Also a rough count of who is talking to us. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: p99 limiter wait
panels.description: Latency the limiter itself adds. This is time we impose, not time we measure, so it is excluded from the native-vs-Synapse comparison. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Rejection share
panels.description: Share of requests refused by the limiter. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Rate limiting by endpoint
panels.description: Rejections and delays per endpoint. There is deliberately no per-origin series: this server has exchanged keys with tens of thousands of others, and a label per origin would be a cardinality explosion. Which server is being limited is in the worker logs, at warn for rejections and info for delays. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

panels.title: Limiter wait time
panels.description: How long requests spend waiting on the limiter, by percentile. Note: gopro_requests_total{status="429"} does not distinguish our rejections from Synapse's 429 relayed through the proxy. To ask whether we rejected anything, read gopro_rate_limited_origins or gopro_rate_limit_slept_total.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.50, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_rate_limit_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le, endpoint) (rate(gopro_rate_limit_queue_wait_seconds_bucket{endpoint=~"$fedread_endpoint", job=~"$job", instance=~"$instance"}[$bucket])))

panels.title: State group hit rate
panels.description: The one that matters. Resolving state at an event is by far the most expensive read; a state group's contents never change, so a hit turns a full recursive walk into a map lookup. Measured cold-vs-warm on the largest room here: 1.04s against 2us.

panels.title: Event hit rate
panels.description: Stored event JSON, which does not change.

panels.title: Cache memory
panels.description: Total across all caches. Compare against the configured bounds.

panels.title: Evictions
panels.description: Entries dropped to stay within the size bound. Sustained evictions on state_groups mean the bound is too small for the working set, and the expensive resolutions are being recomputed.

panels.title: Entries cached
panels.description: Total entries across all caches.

panels.title: Hit rate by cache
panels.description: Fraction of lookups served from memory, since startup. Caches are empty after a restart, so expect this to climb rather than start high.

panels.title: Cache size against bound
panels.description: Bytes held versus the configured limit. A cache pinned at its bound with steady evictions is undersized.

panels.title: Lookups per second
panels.description: Hits and misses by cache.

panels.title: Filtered state from cache
panels.description: Share of /event's filtered state-group lookups answered from cache rather than a recursive walk of state_groups_state. 'filtered_cache' is the per-(group,filter) cache; 'state_cache' means the whole map happened to be resident.

panels.title: Filtered state lookups
panels.description: Filtered state-group resolutions by query kind and source. 'database' means a recursive CTE over state_groups_state; 'cache' means the whole map was already resolved.

panels.title: Invalidation stream
panels.description: The caches serve only while this is Connected. While it is Disconnected they are empty and every request goes to Postgres — a latency cost, never a correctness one.

panels.title: Cache flushes
panels.description: Times the caches were emptied in the window: a purge, a (re)connect, or a row we could not parse. Occasional flushes are normal; a steady stream means the subscription is flapping.

panels.title: Malformed rows
panels.description: Replication rows we failed to parse. Each one empties the caches, because an unparsed row may have been the purge that makes us wrong. Anything above zero means Synapse's format has moved.

panels.title: Replication commands
panels.description: Everything arriving on the channel. RDATA/caches is the one that can affect us; presence and receipts dominate by volume and are ignored.

panels.title: Cache invalidations
panels.description: Invalidation rows by Synapse cache function. ph_cache_fake and dr_cache_fake mean events were deleted and empty every cache; 'ignored' is everything we do not mirror.

panels.title: Invalidation stream age
panels.description: Time since the last replication message. The caches are armed only while this subscription is healthy, so a stream that has gone quiet is the difference between a cache that is safe and one that is silently stale. Quiet periods are normal overnight; hours of silence during European daytime are not.

panels.title: /state_ids computations
panels.description: Whether a request computed its answer, joined an identical computation already in flight, or stopped waiting.

panels.title: Auth chains walked without the index
panels.description: Auth chains computed by recursive walk because the chain cover index was incomplete.

panels.title: Expired origin keys
panels.description: Requests rejected because the origin's published key was past its valid_until_ts.

panels.title: Sending federation
panels.description: 1 while homeserver.yaml names this instance in federation_sender_instances.

panels.title: Replication
panels.description: While this is 0 the worker learns about nothing new. Stream positions are stale.

panels.title: Synapse DB role
panels.description: Whether the connection to Synapse's database can write. The sender must be able to: its cursor is a set of deletions.

panels.title: Destinations known
panels.description: Queues that exist. Grows to this worker's share of the destination list and stops.

panels.title: Backing off
panels.description: Destinations refusing to be dialled. A large number is NORMAL — a homeserver's destination list is mostly a graveyard. Watch its SHAPE: a step change means a problem at our end, not theirs.

panels.title: Version
panels.description: Build stamped at compile time.

panels.title: Events examined per second
panels.description: Examined counts every event the pickup loop looked at; routed counts those that produced at least one destination in this shard. Most events are remote-origin and are correctly skipped, so the gap between the two lines is expected and large.

panels.title: Transactions per second
panels.description: Transactions this worker put on the wire. One shard's worth: what this worker owns is sha256(destination) mod len(federation_sender_instances).

panels.title: PDUs and EDUs per second
panels.description:
PDUs and EDUs put on the wire, with EDUs broken down by type to match Synapse's synapse_federation_client_sent_edus_by_type_total.

'states per presence EDU' is the one to read after a change to presence handling. One m.presence EDU carries up to 50 users, so this at 1.0 means every user is costing a transaction of its own -- an HTTP request and a signature verification on somebody else's server, per person. Above 1.0 means presence is merging.

Read it WITH the 'presence states' line, not instead of it: merging shows as the m.presence line falling while presence states holds steady. If states falls too, presence is being lost rather than merged, and the ratio alone cannot tell the difference.

panels.title: Events skipped, by reason
panels.description: Shape matters more than height. 'remote origin' dominating is correct — most traffic is other servers' events. A filter that suddenly rejects everything shows up here as a change in composition, not merely a drop in throughput.

panels.title: Event processing lag (p50 / p95 / p99)
panels.description: Seconds from an event being persisted to this worker finishing routing it. The headline number for a sender: it is what a user waits for.

panels.title: Where the time goes, per stage (p95)
panels.description: p95 per stage, over a ONE HOUR window rather than the dashboard's rate interval. That is deliberate. This worker routes on the order of one event a minute, so a short window leaves histogram_quantile interpolating inside a bucket from two or three samples -- which produced a confident '4.20 s' for a stage whose p95 across its whole history was 24 ms. The sample rate is plotted alongside for the same reason: a quantile computed from almost nothing should be visibly computed from almost nothing.

panels.title: Fan-out duration (p50 / p95 / p99)
panels.description: Time to hand one event to every destination queue in this shard. The number the whole design is a bet on.

panels.title: Destinations per routed event
panels.description: The fan-out width -- how many servers one event has to reach. One goroutine each is the bet this worker is built on, so this is the load that bet is taken against.

panels.title: State group cache hit rate
panels.description: The joined-host lookup is the most expensive thing in the per-event path -- a recursive walk of the state group edges, hundreds of milliseconds on a deep chain and seconds at worst. A state group is immutable, so the answer is cached with no invalidation and the query runs once per state CHANGE rather than once per event. Events between two state changes share a group (14.5 of them here, measured), so expect a high rate; a falling one means rooms are changing membership faster than the cache holds them, or that it is too small. 'entries held' against resolution.host_cache_entries answers whether a bigger cache would help: while it sits below the limit nothing has been evicted, so every miss is a first sight of a state group and raising the limit changes nothing.

panels.title: Queued work
panels.description: Sampled rather than tracked by counter, so a leak shows up even when the counters that should have caught it are themselves the buggy part. Steady growth means delivery is not keeping up with routing.

panels.title: Send duration by outcome (p95)
panels.description: Labelled by outcome because a fast failure and a fast success are indistinguishable in a duration histogram — a remote that refuses instantly would otherwise read as excellent performance.

panels.title: Sends in flight
panels.description: Against queue.max_concurrent_destinations. Pinned at the bound means the concurrency limit, not the network, is what is pacing delivery.

panels.title: Replication rows by stream
panels.description: A stream that stops arriving is invisible everywhere else: the worker simply has less to do and looks healthy.

panels.title: Events stream position
panels.description: How far through the events stream this worker has read. A stream ordering of ONE homeserver: it counts that server's events and means nothing next to another deployment's number.

panels.title: Approximate routes, by cause
panels.description:
Routing decisions that fell back to CURRENT room state instead of resolving the state before the event.

'forked dag' is work not done here -- full state resolution is room-sized. It should be rare; a rising line means events are being routed from a state that is close, not exact.

panels.title: Outbound federation: Bookkeeping written to Synapse's tables
Write operations per second
panels.description: The sender's bookkeeping: the deletions and cursor writes that are its position. A flat zero here while events flow and Sending federation is 1 means the sender is not recording what it delivered, and a restart would replay it.

panels.title: Write failures
panels.description: Non-zero here means delivery is working while the bookkeeping is not: rows are re-read forever, the outbox grows without bound, and prev_id chaining silently lags. Nothing else reports it.

panels.title: Query rate by name
panels.description: Every query this worker makes, measured at the POOL rather than at chosen call sites -- the query nobody thought to time is the one that turns out to be slow. A query with no name is counted as 'other', so an uninstrumented one shows as a rising line rather than as nothing.

panels.title: Query duration p95 by name
panels.description: Over an hour, because this worker makes few queries of some kinds and a short window leaves histogram_quantile interpolating from two or three samples. joined_hosts_at_state_group is the one to watch: it walks the state group edges and was measured against this database at 10.8ms, 108ms, 375ms and 6.3 SECONDS for the deepest chain.

panels.title: Query errors
panels.description: By pool and name. A fast error is the fastest query there is, so a failing query looks like excellent performance in the duration panel and shows up only here.

panels.title: Connection pool
panels.description: The resource this worker contends on with itself: a thousand destination goroutines resolving rooms queue for the same database.max_conns connections. Acquired pinned at max is the signal -- and it means 'slow query' and 'waited for a connection' need telling apart, because they are fixed differently.

panels.title: Waiting for a connection
panels.description: Time spent waiting because the pool was empty, and how often that happened. Flat means the pool is big enough; a rising line means raising database.max_conns will do more than optimising any query.

panels.title: Destinations
panels.description: Backing off is normal for dead servers; the backoff here reaches a year.

panels.title: Transaction bytes
panels.description: Bytes of transaction body assembled.

panels.title: Refused with 429, top 10 destinations
panels.description: Transactions a destination refused with 429. A cooldown, not a backoff.

panels.title: EDUs dropped, top 10 destinations
panels.description: Ephemeral EDUs (typing, presence, receipts) dropped because the destination is in a long outage. Normal for dead servers.

panels.title: Events created
panels.description: Events built here and persisted by the events writer, over the window.

panels.title: Verify mismatches
panels.description: Native events that differ from what the events writer persisted. Anything but 0 is a parity bug.

panels.title: Handed to main
panels.description: Event-creation requests left to main before anything was written.

panels.title: Refused here
panels.description: Requests refused natively, in Synapse's words.

panels.title: Requests by how they were served
panels.description: native: answered here; fallback: the creator looked and left it to main; proxy: a read under the creator's paths that nginx sent here.

panels.title: Requests by room class and status
panels.description: Every room ID counts as allowlisted (the series continue from goevent-creator, which ran rooms: all); alias is a join or knock by alias.

panels.title: Native results
panels.description: What each native request came to: created, deduplicated, refused, delayed.

panels.title: Handed to main, by reason
panels.description: Why requests were left to main. The share should shrink, never grow.

panels.title: Refusals, by reason
panels.description: Refusals given here; each is Synapse's status, errcode and words.

panels.title: Verify results
panels.description: Each native event checked against what was persisted, by check.

panels.title: Native latency (p50, p95)
panels.description: From the request to the answer, the events writer included.

panels.title: Profile writes and their join events
panels.description: Profile fields set here, and the join events each change sends into the user's rooms (resumed after a restart from goevent_profile_propagations).

panels.title: Event creator: Main and the events writer
Main's latency for handed-over requests (p50, p95)
panels.description: A remote join can take minutes; upstream.timeout_seconds bounds it.

panels.title: send_events to the events writer
panels.description: Time to persist through send_events, retries included, and how often by result.

panels.title: Replication retries
panels.description: Requests to the events writer, main or the profile writer retried after a timeout or a connection failure.
